q: Which rhythms does this recap say the AED is looking for?

opts.why: The AED looks for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia.
Asystole (flatline) is not shockable. The AED looks for VF and pulseless VT.
No-shock rhythms are not what the AED is looking to treat with a shock.
The shockable pair in this recap is VF and pulseless VT.

q: The AED says no shock advised. What do you do?

opts.why: No shock advised means it is not VF/VT. Resume CPR immediately.
Do not wait without compressions.
Keep the AED on and keep CPR going.
Stay clear only for analysis or shock. After no-shock, resume CPR.

q: Why hands off while the AED analyzes?

opts.why: If you are touching them, the AED may pick up your heart rhythm.
Hands off is so it reads their rhythm, not because it is charging pads.
The prompt is for rhythm analysis, not a pad-stick check.
Stop touching for analysis. Resume compressions after.

q: Standard adult AED pad placement in this recap?

opts.why: One pad upper right chest, one pad lower left chest, along the heart’s path.
That reverses the path. It is upper right and lower left.
Adult default is anterior-lateral, not both on the back.
Front-back is for a child or infant who is too small, not the adult default.

q: Child or infant too small for adult pad placement. Where do the pads go?

opts.why: Anterior-posterior: one pad center of the chest, one pad center of the back.
That adult placement is only if the child is big enough.
One is on the chest and one is on the back.
Front-back is chest and back, not both on the chest.

q: No pediatric pads. The patient is a child who needs a shock. What pads?

opts.why: No pediatric pads? Use adult pads. More electricity than needed beats none.
Do not skip a needed shock. Use adult pads.
Do not wait. Adult pads on the child.
Do not hold for pediatric energy. Adult pads on the child.

q: There is a pacemaker bump under the skin. Where does the pad go?

opts.why: Do not place a pad on the device. Move it about 1 inch (2–3 cm) away.
Do not park a pad on the pacemaker or ICD.
You still place both pads. Shift the one near the bump.

q: What compression rate does this recap want?

opts.why: 100–120 per minute. Faster than 120 drops quality. Not just “at least 100.”
There is a cap. Over 120 reduces quality.
That is too slow. The band is 100–120.
That is too fast. Stay at 100–120.

q: Adult compression depth in this recap?

opts.why: Adults: at least 2 inches (5 cm). Allow full recoil.
1.5 inches is the infant ballpark, not the adult depth.
4 inches is too deep for this recap’s adult number.
Adult depth is at least 2 inches, not 1 inch.

q: You are the only one doing CPR (partner is getting the AED). Ratio?

opts.why: Single rescuer is 30:2 for all ages. Two-rescuer 15:2 is only when two people are actually doing CPR.
15:2 is two-rescuer CPR on a child or infant, not a solo rescuer.
If you are alone on CPR, a child is still 30:2.
That split is two-rescuer CPR. Solo is 30:2 for every age.

q: Two people are actually doing CPR on a child. Ratio?

opts.why: Two-rescuer CPR on children and infants is 15:2. Adults stay 30:2.
30:2 is single-rescuer (all ages) or two-rescuer adults, not two-rescuer child.
The two breaths stay. It is 15:2, not 15:1.
Two-rescuer child is 15:2, not 30:1.

q: They are in pooled water. What does this recap want before you shock?

opts.why: Water conducts. Move them out of pooled water. A quick wipe of damp skin is enough.
They do not need to be bone dry. Wipe and shock on dry ground.
Still use the AED after you move them out of the water.
A wipe is for damp skin, not pooled water. Move them out first.
